regions.labelEs: A VECES, MIS CONVERSACIONES CON DESCONOCIDOS SE PROLONGAN DURANTE UN RATO ANTES DE DARME CUENTA DE QUE ESTÁN HABLANDO POR TELÉFONO.

applications.explanationEn: A veces marks the behavior as happening on some occasions rather than every time.
Antes de introduces the earlier boundary, and dar remains in its unchanged -ar dictionary form inside darme.
Me attaches to the end of the unchanged dictionary form dar and is written as part of the same word.
Me is attached to dar for the speaker, cuenta completes the realization expression, and de que opens the fact being noticed.
Están changes for the plural subject, while hablar becomes hablando with the action ending -ando.
Hablando is the current form of the action, and por teléfono names the channel used for it.
Qué keeps its written accent because it asks a direct question here.
Qué and hay form the complete casual greeting rather than a request to list things that exist.

excludedUnits.rationale: Bernanke is an English-language personal proper name retained unchanged, not a Spanish lexical word.

applications.explanationEn: Cómo keeps its written accent because the graph label asks about a degree.
Cómo de opens the degree question, and a menudo supplies the frequency expression whose degree is being measured.
A and menudo form the fixed frequency expression together.

Incómoda uses feminine singular -a to match zona.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word; part of a veces, “sometimes”

cards.questionEn: How do you say “sometimes” in Spanish?
cards.noteEn: This common time expression describes something that happens on some occasions but not always. It normally sits before or after the verb without changing form.
In frequency expressions such as a veces and algunas veces, English commonly translates the whole expression as “sometimes.”

cards.answerEn: strangers; people one does not know
cards.noteEn: Desconocidos can describe unknown people or things. Used by itself for people, it is a plural noun meaning strangers; the masculine plural form can refer to a mixed group.

example.en: I do not usually talk to strangers.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word; makes prolongan mean ‘go on’ or ‘drag on’
cards.noteEn: Prolongarse uses a matching small marker with the person or thing that continues longer: me, te, se, nos, os, or se. Here se goes with a plural subject and makes the conversations themselves continue, without naming anyone who deliberately extends them.

cards.answerEn: go on; drag on; last longer
cards.noteEn: Prolongan is the present-time plural form of prolongar. With se before it, prolongarse describes several things continuing longer rather than someone deliberately extending them.

example.en: The meetings drag on too long.

cards.noteEn: Durante introduces a period of time. Natural English often uses ‘for’ before a measured duration, such as an hour, but ‘during’ before a named event or period, such as the meeting.

cards.answerEn: while; a short or unspecified period of time
cards.noteEn: Un rato refers to an imprecise stretch of time. Its length depends on the situation rather than on a fixed number of minutes.
Before a full event with its own verb, antes normally begins the connector antes de que.

cards.promptEs: antes de + verbo en forma de diccionario
cards.questionEn: How do you say that one action happens before another action by the same person?
cards.answerEn: Use antes de, then keep the second action verb in its unchanged dictionary form.
cards.noteEn: The dictionary form is the unchanged form ending in -ar, -er, or -ir, such as salir, comer, or escribir. Use antes de directly before that form when no new subject is named. If the later action has its own stated subject, Spanish normally uses antes de que and a different verb form.

example.es: Apaga la luz antes de salir.
example.en: Turn off the light before leaving.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word; links antes to the following action
cards.noteEn: Keep de after antes when the next action stays in its unchanged dictionary form: antes de salir. English expresses the sequence with 'before' and does not translate de separately.

example.es: Lávate las manos antes de comer.

cards.answerEn: to realize; to notice (as part of darme cuenta)
cards.noteEn: Darme joins the unchanged dictionary form dar, normally ‘to give,’ to me. In darme cuenta, the two words form the fixed expression ‘to realize’ or ‘to notice’; me identifies the speaker as the person who realizes something.

example.es: Tardé en darme cuenta del error.
example.en: It took me a while to notice the error.

cards.promptEs: verbo en forma de diccionario + pronombre unido
cards.questionEn: Where can a short object word such as me, te, lo, or la go with an unchanged action verb?
cards.answerEn: Attach it to the end of the verb and write the result as one word.
cards.noteEn: An unchanged dictionary-form verb ends in -ar, -er, or -ir. Short object words can attach directly: conocer + te becomes conocerte, and ayudar + me becomes ayudarme.

cards.promptEs: darse cuenta de (que) + hecho o situación
cards.questionEn: How do you say that someone realizes or becomes aware of something?
cards.answerEn: Use the matching small pronoun, a form of dar, cuenta, and then de before what is realized.
cards.noteEn: The small pronoun and dar must match the person: me doy cuenta, te das cuenta, se da cuenta, nos damos cuenta, and so on. Use de before a noun and de que before a full statement. Cuenta is not translated separately in this expression.

example.es: Nos dimos cuenta de que faltaba una llave.
example.en: We realized that a key was missing.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word; completes darse cuenta, “to realize”
cards.noteEn: Cuenta can mean an account, bill, or calculation. In darse cuenta, it is part of a fixed expression and is not translated separately.

example.es: Ella se dio cuenta muy tarde.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word here; introduces what is realized after darse cuenta
cards.noteEn: After darse cuenta, de introduces the fact or thing that becomes clear. Before a full statement, Spanish normally uses de que.

example.es: Se dio cuenta de que era tarde.
example.en: She realized that it was late.

cards.noteEn: Que introduces a clause after verbs such as creer, saber, esperar, or decir. English often uses “that,” but may leave it unstated.

example.en: I think that Ana is coming.

cards.answerEn: they are (helping to describe an action in progress)
cards.noteEn: Here están is the plural form of estar used before an action ending in -ando or -iendo.

cards.answerEn: Use a form of estar followed by an action word ending in -ando or -iendo.
cards.noteEn: Estar changes to show who is doing the action: estoy, estás, está, and so on. For most verbs, replace -ar with -ando (hablar → hablando) and replace -er or -ir with -iendo (comer → comiendo, vivir → viviendo). This is similar to English “am/is/are doing.”
cards.questionEn: How do you say that someone is in the middle of doing something?

cards.noteEn: Hablando is the -ando action form of hablar, “to speak.” This form can add an action happening at the same time.

example.en: He left while talking on the phone.

cards.questionEn: How do you say that someone talks to another person on the phone?
cards.answerEn: Use the matching form of hablar followed by por teléfono.
cards.noteEn: Hablar changes for the person and time. Por teléfono stays together to name the communication channel; Spanish uses por here where natural English normally says ‘on the phone.’ Add con plus a person when you want to name the other participant.

example.es: Lucía habla por teléfono con su hermano.
example.en: Lucía talks with her brother on the phone.

cards.noteEn: Por can identify the channel used to communicate: por teléfono, por radio, or por videollamada. Natural English often uses ‘on,’ ‘by,’ or ‘over’ rather than translating por with one fixed word.
Teléfono is stressed on lé, which is why it carries a written accent.

cards.answerEn: Write qué, cómo, cuándo, and similar words with an accent when they ask a question or add an exclamation.
cards.noteEn: This includes direct questions (¿Qué quieres?), questions inside another sentence (No sé qué quiere), and exclamations (¡Qué bonito!). Without the accent, these words usually connect parts of a sentence instead: el libro que quiero means “the book that I want.”
cards.questionEn: Why do words such as que, como, and cuando sometimes have a written accent?
How can you casually ask someone ‘What's up?’
cards.answerEn: Use ¿Qué hay? as a casual greeting or conversation opener.
cards.noteEn: Qué carries an accent because it asks a question, and hay normally means ‘there is’ or ‘there are.’ Together, ¿Qué hay? literally asks what there is, but in casual conversation it works like ‘What's up?’ The tone is informal.

cards.answerEn: is up; is going on (as part of ¿qué hay?)
cards.noteEn: Hay ordinarily means ‘there is’ or ‘there are.’ In the fixed casual question ¿Qué hay?, it helps ask ‘What's up?’ or ‘What's going on?’ rather than literally asking for an inventory.
Eh can fill a pause while a speaker thinks or reacts. Its tone and punctuation determine whether it sounds hesitant, surprised, or attention-getting.

example.en: Um... I need to think about it.

cards.noteEn: Mucho can stand by itself when the kind of amount is already clear. It then means ‘much’ or ‘a lot’ without a following noun.

cards.promptEs: cómo de + palabra o expresión de grado
cards.questionEn: How can you ask to what degree a quality applies, especially in Spain?
cards.answerEn: Use cómo de before the word or expression that describes the degree.
cards.noteEn: Cómo carries an accent because it asks a question, and de stays fixed after it. The following description stays in its normal form: cómo de lejos, cómo de rápido, or cómo de a menudo. This pattern is especially common in Spain; many speakers elsewhere use qué tan instead, while cuán sounds more formal.

example.en: How far away is the station?

cards.answerEn: no separate English word; links cómo to the degree being asked about
cards.noteEn: This de is the fixed middle piece of cómo de, a construction especially common in Spain for asking how strongly a description applies.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word; begins a menudo, ‘often’
cards.noteEn: The a is required in the fixed expression a menudo. It does not introduce a destination or a person here.

cards.questionEn: How do you say that something happens often?
cards.answerEn: Use a menudo before or after the action.
cards.noteEn: A menudo is a fixed two-word expression for frequent events. Keep the opening a; menudo does not change for the person or thing involved. Its position is flexible, but placing it at the start often gives the frequency extra emphasis.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word; completes a menudo, ‘often’
cards.noteEn: Menudo has other uses on its own, but after a it forms the fixed frequency expression a menudo. Learn the two words together for ‘often.’

cards.questionEn: Where does a basic Spanish describing word usually go relative to its noun?
cards.answerEn: Put it after the noun in the common neutral order.
cards.noteEn: Many ordinary descriptive words follow the person or thing they describe: un coche rojo, una casa grande. Some adjectives commonly come before the noun, and moving an adjective can change emphasis or meaning, so this is a useful default rather than an absolute rule.

cards.promptEs: adjetivo que concuerda con masculino o femenino
cards.questionEn: How does a Spanish describing word change for a man, woman, or gendered noun?
cards.answerEn: Make the describing word match the gender and number of the person or thing it describes.
cards.noteEn: Many describing words ending in -o change to -a for a feminine singular person or noun: cansado becomes cansada. Plurals normally add -s. Some describing words have one form for both genders.

example.es: Pedro está cansado y Ana está cansada.
example.en: Pedro is tired and Ana is tired.

cards.promptEs: número ordinal antes de un sustantivo
cards.questionEn: How do you use words such as first, second, or third before a Spanish noun?
cards.answerEn: Put the ordinal before the noun and make its ending match the noun's gender and number.
cards.noteEn: An ordinal gives a position in an order. Primero, segundo, tercero, último, and similar words usually come before the noun. Most forms use -o with a masculine singular noun and -a with a feminine singular noun, but primero and tercero shorten to primer and tercer before a masculine singular noun. Plural nouns use plural forms.

example.es: La segunda puerta está en el tercer piso.
example.en: The second door is on the third floor.
